title: How should you prepare for a case interview in three weeks?
description: The usual run-up? A simple, realistic plan for 21 days of case interview prep, with what to do each week.
hook: In three weeks, spend week one learning the course and the core frameworks with an easy case every other day, week two doing a case and a drill every day plus your first case with a friend, and week three practising hard cases against the clock, two more with a friend, and your fit stories. Three weeks is the most common run-up to a case interview, and it is plenty if each week has a clear job. Here is the plan, with two checkpoints that tell you where to spend your time.
body:
In this guide

  • The plan at a glance
  • Week 1: learn the method
  • Week 2: build volume and fix weak spots
  • Week 3: make it realistic
  • Two checkpoints that steer the plan
  • Focused sprints for any weak skill
  • A sample day in week two
  • Mistakes that waste three weeks
  • If you fall behind
  • Check yourself

The plan at a glance

WeekMain jobCasesTime per day
1The whole course and the 11 frameworksAn easy case every other day (3 or 4)About 1 hour
2A case a day, a drill a day5 to 7, including your first with a friendAbout 1.5 hours
3Hard cases against the clock, fit stories5 to 6, including two with a friendAbout 1.5 hours

That adds up to roughly 13 to 17 cases, enough to see every common case type at least twice. If you set your interview date on PrepForCase, your home page shows which week you are in.

Week 1: learn the method

Work through the eleven lessons of the free course, two or three a day. They take about ten minutes each, so you will finish by midweek. Then learn the 11 frameworks: not to recite, but to recognise which shape a prompt calls for. Read the phrases for each stage once and say them out loud.

Alongside this, do an easy case every other day. Choose ones with a clear structure, such as a straightforward profitability or market entry case from the casebook. The aim is to practise the flow (recap, clarify, structure, analyse, recommend), not to impress anyone. Do your first case out loud even if it feels awkward; the awkwardness is information.

Start one habit this week that runs all the way to the interview: ten minutes of mental maths a day in the maths drill.

Week 2: build volume and fix weak spots

Now do one full case every day, followed by a ten-minute drill aimed at your weakest skill. Mix case types deliberately: profitability, market entry, M&A or investment, pricing, growth and one with a market sizing.

Do your first case with another person this week. It does not need to be a consultant. A friend reading from the casebook's interviewer script will still interrupt, ask you to explain yourself and hand you exhibits when you ask for them, which is what solo practice cannot do. Practising with a partner explains how to set it up.

After every case, write one fix in your case log. Read the last five before you start the next case.

Week 3: make it realistic

This week is about performing under realistic conditions:

  • Hard cases against the clock. Pick cases with ambiguous prompts, several exhibits or industries you know little about. Give yourself about 30 minutes, the same as a real case.
  • Maths out loud, on paper, without a calculator. Live case interviews do not allow one.
  • Two cases with a friend, ideally someone who will push back. Ask them to throw in one surprise fact mid-case.
  • Fit stories. Build six to eight with the fit interview guide and rehearse two a day. Have a partner ask at least one deep follow-up on each: "What exactly did you say? What would you do differently?"

Keep the day before the interview light: read your fixes, rehearse two stories, check logistics and rest. On the morning, use the 30-minute warm-up.

Two checkpoints that steer the plan

Checkpoint 1: end of week one

Try a case you have never seen without looking at any framework sheet. Ask a partner, or your own recording, to score three things separately: did you get the objective right, was the structure complete and tailored, and was the maths right. Spend the drill time in week two on the weakest of the three rather than splitting it evenly out of habit.

Checkpoint 2: end of week two

Do a case in an unfamiliar industry with a demanding partner. The question is whether you can adapt a framework instead of reproducing the last case's branches. If your structure for a hospital waiting-list case looked suspiciously like your structure for a retailer's profits, week three should include more unusual prompts, such as public sector and operations cases.

Track progress with evidence, not feelings. "Identified whether revenue or costs drove the drop before brainstorming" is progress you can see. "Felt better" is not.

Focused sprints for any weak skill

When one skill lags, give it a five-day sprint inside your daily drill time.

Weak skillFive-day sprint
Structure and hypothesis30 structures, two minutes each, compared with the model, in the structuring drill
Maths and charts30 chart reads at 90 seconds each in the chart drill, plus ten minutes of speed maths a day
RecommendationTen recorded 60-second closes; count filler words, then re-record answer-first
Clarify and recap20 case openings: recap and three questions only, graded by a partner
Case leadershipFive cases where you announce the next step after every answer; your partner tallies each time you wait
CommunicationDaily voice exercises from the speaking guide plus one recorded full case

A sample day in week two

  1. 2 minutes: read your last five case-log fixes.
  2. 35 minutes: one full case, out loud.
  3. 10 minutes: review. Score the six skills and write one new fix.
  4. 10 minutes: sprint drill for your weakest skill.
  5. 10 minutes: mental maths.
  6. 15 minutes: draft or rehearse one fit story.

That is 82 minutes. On days you cannot manage it, keep the case and the review and drop the rest.

Mistakes that waste three weeks

  • Spending week one reading. Lessons and frameworks matter, but if you have not spoken a case out loud by day three, you are behind.
  • Only doing comfortable case types. Keep a tally and fill the gaps.
  • Never practising with a person. Solo practice will not prepare you for interruptions.
  • Leaving fit to the last two days. Good stories take time to find. Start listing candidates in week two.
  • Peaking too early. Ten cases in the final three days leaves you tired, not sharp.

If you fall behind

You will miss a day. Everyone does. Do not double up the next day; pick up where the plan is today. If you lose several days, protect week three's realistic practice and fit preparation, and trim week two's volume.

Check yourself

1. At checkpoint 1 your objective and maths were fine, but your structure missed a whole branch. What changes in week two?

Show the answer

Put your drill time into structuring: six two-minute structures a day, compared against model answers, with a check after each one for anything missing. Keep the daily case as it is.

2. You have done 14 cases by the end of week three, all profitability or market entry. Is that a problem?

Show the answer

Yes. You have volume but not range. In the remaining days, swap in M&A, pricing, operations and a public sector case so an unfamiliar prompt does not throw you.

3. How many minutes of mental maths will you have done if you drill ten minutes a day for all 21 days?

Show the answer

21 × 10 = 210 minutes, three and a half hours, which is enough to make percentages, growth and big-number multiplication feel routine.

Where to go next

Start week one with lesson 1. If your interview moves closer, switch to the one-week plan; if it moves further away, the six-week plan gives you more room to build.
